tour.title: Palaces, Hanok & Scholar's Lanes: Gyeongbokgung to Insadong
tour.summary: A royal palace rebuilt from its own ruins, a hillside village of traditional houses arguing with its tourists, and an old art street that sells the past back to the country that demolished it.
tour.overviewText:
Seoul in early January runs on two clocks. On the surface it is a cold, fast, modern capital: eight-lane roads, delivery scooters, subways running past midnight. Underneath, it keeps the hours of a dynasty that governed this peninsula for five hundred years. This walk runs through the seam between the two. Bring your warmest coat — the winter light is thin and sharp, the courtyards are nearly empty in the morning, and a dusting of snow turns a palace roof into the picture everyone comes for.

Start with the country. South Korea is a democracy of about fifty million people that went from one of the poorest nations on earth in the 1950s to one of the richest in three generations, mostly by exporting things — ships, cars, semiconductors, pop music. Seoul is its capital, and about half the country lives in its sprawl. The dynasty is Joseon, founded in 1392 by a general named Yi Seong-gye, who took the throne name Taejo, moved the capital here in 1394 and built the palace you are about to walk through a year later. Joseon governed less by divine right than by Confucian procedure: an exam, a graded bureaucracy, and a calendar of rituals that decided who stood where. Confucian duties, Buddhist practice and older shamanic habits have coexisted inside the same Korean family for centuries. The state that enforced them is gone; some of it is still legible in stone.

The twentieth century broke it. Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled it as a colony until 1945; at this palace the colonial government demolished most of the buildings for an industrial exhibition in 1915, then planted its own head office in front of the throne hall in 1926. That building came down in 1995 and 1996, and the palace has been under reconstruction ever since — a project due to finish around 2045. A kilometre east, in the alleys of Bukchon, a quieter version of that argument is live: who gets to live in a preserved neighbourhood, and how many visitors a residential street can absorb. In Insadong, where the walk ends, heritage has become an industry — tea, brushes, handmade paper and calligraphy, sold as a version of the country that the country itself knocked down.

The route is simple: north through the palace from Gwanghwamun Square, then east and up into the hillside lanes of Samcheong-dong and Bukchon, and finally down to Insadong for tea. Mostly downhill after the first climb.

Practicals, plainly. The walk is about 4.2 kilometres, roughly fifty minutes on your feet. The palace is closed every Tuesday, and the first two hours of this walk are inside it: a Tuesday is a wasted day. Adult admission is ₩3,000 (the won, ₩, is the local currency; roughly 1,300–1,400 to the US dollar), children aged 7 to 18 pay ₩1,500, and under-sixes, over-65s and anyone in a hanbok — traditional Korean dress, rented cheaply nearby — walk in free. In December and January the palace closes at 17:30 with last admission at 16:30, so start early; 10:00, when the guard changes, is the clock to set. Verify every fee and hour at the gate.

Come for the throne hall. Stay for the stone marker that tells you where a sixth-rank official was required to stand.
tour.difficulty: Easy to moderate. Level, paved palace courtyards and city pavements, with one real climb into the hillside lanes of Samcheong-dong and Bukchon, and a long descent to Insadong. The hanok alleys are steep and narrow and genuinely slippery once snow or ice settles; the palace courtyards are broad and step-free but the distances add up.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Set off around 09:30 so you are standing in front of Gwanghwamun for the 10:00 changing of the royal guard, then give the palace two and a half hours. In late December and early January the sun sets about 17:20 and the palace shuts at 17:30, so the whole walk has to happen inside a short day; Samcheong-dong and Bukchon are best in the early afternoon, and Insadong's tea houses are at their warmest as it gets dark. Avoid Tuesdays entirely — the palace is closed.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Full attribution for each image appears on its stop page and in Settings.

stops.name: Gwanghwamun Square
stops.narration:
Begin where modern Korea argues with itself. Two bronze men stand on this square, and between them they explain most of what the country believes about its own history. The nearer, seated figure is King Sejong the Great, who reigned from 1418 to 1450, the fourth king of the Joseon dynasty, the state that ruled this peninsula from 1392 until Japan annexed it in 1910. He is here for one achievement: in 1443 he created Hangul, the Korean alphabet. Before it, Korean was written with Chinese characters and literacy belonged to an educated elite. Hangul is featural, meaning the shapes of several consonants are drawn from the position your tongue, lips and throat take when you say them, and a motivated adult can learn to read it in an afternoon. That is why Koreans describe it not as a script but as a gift to the poor.

The further statue, standing, is Admiral Yi Sun-sin (1545–1598), who defeated Japanese fleets in the Imjin War, the invasions of Korea from 1592 to 1598, with a fleet including the armour-plated "turtle ships," and died in the final battle; it was put up in 1968. The plaza itself was rebuilt in 2022 into the wide green strip you see. It is Seoul's living room and its protest ground, and has been both in the same decade: candlelight demonstrations that filled this road in 2016 and 2017 led to the impeachment and removal of President Park Geun-hye.

Beneath Sejong's statue is a free exhibition hall, "The Story of King Sejong," open roughly 10:00 to 18:30 and closed Mondays. This square is also the southern anchor of the palace's ceremonial axis. Then turn north: the palace's main gate is a little over 400 metres away.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free, open public square. The small exhibition hall under the statue of King Sejong is normally free but keeps short, changeable hours — verify at its entrance.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. The exhibition hall beneath the square is typically around 10:00 to 18:30 and closed Mondays; check before counting on it.
stops.accessibility: Level, paved and step-free throughout, with the subway station directly beneath and benches along the green strip. Excellent wheeled access.
stops.insiderTip: Stand at the statue of King Sejong and look north: the whole tour is visible from here as a single line — Gwanghwamun, the palace courtyards, and Inwangsan mountain behind. Pick out the north–south axis now and you will understand the palace layout before you walk it.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north across the square, a little over 400 metres, toward the big stone gateway with three arches and a wooden pavilion on top. That is Gwanghwamun, the main gate of the palace — our next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Republic of Korea, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Gwanghwamun Gate
stops.narration:
Three arches, a granite base, a two-storey painted timber pavilion on top, and a name meaning roughly "the king's great virtue illuminates the whole country." This is the front door of Gyeongbokgung, the Palace of Great Fortune, built in 1395 by Yi Seong-gye, the general who took the throne as King Taejo and moved his capital here a year earlier. The arches were a hierarchy in stone: centre for the king, sides for the crown prince and officials. The blue-green-red painted beams are dancheong, a pigment layer that both dresses the building and preserves the wood. Find the haetae, the mythical lion-dogs standing guard, kept here because they were believed to eat fire.

Almost none of what you see is original. The gate burned in the Imjin War, the invasions of 1592 to 1598, and stood ruined for more than two centuries until the 1860s reconstruction. Japan then annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled it until 1945; the colonial government demolished most of the palace for an industrial exhibition in 1915 and in 1926 built its own headquarters in front of the throne hall. The gate was shifted, wrecked again in the Korean War, rebuilt in concrete in 1968, then taken apart and rebuilt in wood and granite between 2006 and 2010 and unveiled on 15 August 2010, Liberation Day.

At 10:00 and 14:00, about twenty minutes each, the royal watch changes on the stone platform in front of you, the woldae, buried for a century. Not on Tuesdays, when the palace shuts. The ceremony was reconstructed in 1996 but researched: the sumunjang, the gate officers, the soldiers under them, and the chwirachi, the military band with drums and conch horns. It is free to watch from outside, though heavy snow or rain can cancel the full ceremony.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Watching the gate and the guard ceremony from outside is free. To pass through into the palace you need the admission ticket, ₩3,000 for adults and ₩1,500 for ages 7 to 18, with under-sixes, over-65s and anyone in hanbok free. Verify at the gate; prices and free-entry rules change.
stops.openingHours: Palace open daily except Tuesdays. In November to January it runs roughly 09:00 to 17:30 with last admission at 16:30 — earlier than in summer. The guard-changing ceremony runs at 10:00 and 14:00, about 20 minutes, Tuesdays excepted. Verify the day's schedule and hours at the gate, and check around New Year, when holiday arrangements can shift.
stops.accessibility: The approach is level pavement. Passage through the gate is flat and wide enough for a wheelchair; the timber pavilion above is reached by internal steps and is not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Stand to one side of the central arch rather than at the barrier in front of it. The ceremony walks through the gate, and from the flank you see the guards' formation — and get out of the crowd's way before everyone surges into the palace at once.
stops.nextStopDirections: Go through the gate and straight on for about 330 metres, through the second gate, Heungnyemun, and across the long stone courtyard behind it. The great hall on its two-tiered stone platform, straight ahead on the central axis, is Geunjeongjeon — our next stop. Your ticket is checked just past Gwanghwamun.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Huntsmanleader, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Geunjeongjeon, the Throne Hall
stops.narration:
Geunjeongjeon means the Hall of Diligent Governance, a warning to the king as much as a boast. Here the dynasty did its public business: royal audiences, the reception of foreign envoys, the proclamation of decrees, coronations. It is Korea's National Treasure number 223, and a rebuilt building, twice over. The first version went up in 1395 with the palace; it burned in 1592, when the Japanese invasions destroyed Gyeongbokgung, and lay in ruins for more than 270 years. The hall you see was completed in 1867, under the regent Heungseon Daewongun, father of King Gojong.

Now look at the floor, because here the Joseon state becomes visible. The hall sits on a two-tiered stone platform, the woldae, and along the courtyard edges stand rows of small stone markers, the pumgyeseok, each carrying the name of a government office and a rank. On ceremonial days every official took his assigned place at the stone matching his grade, civil officials east and military west, so the whole hierarchy of the kingdom stood arranged in front of the throne. Confucian governance was not only a philosophy; it was a seating plan, carved in granite. A sixth-rank official stood where the sixth-rank stone was, and everyone knew it.

Go up the steps and look at the throne. Behind it is a folding screen painted with a red sun, a white moon and five craggy peaks: irworobongdo, the painting of the sun, moon and five peaks, which stood behind every Joseon king. The sun and moon are king and queen, the peaks a mythic mountain, a claim that the throne sat at the centre of a balanced cosmos. Propaganda, and beautiful. The pavilion on the water, about 250 metres away, is where the dynasty relaxed.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Covered by the palace admission ticket — ₩3,000 adult, ₩1,500 ages 7 to 18, free for under-sixes, over-65s, hanbok wearers and on Culture Day, the last Wednesday of each month. Verify prices and free-entry rules at the gate; they change, and the interior of the hall is sometimes roped off for conservation.
stops.openingHours: In step with the palace: daily except Tuesdays. November to January roughly 09:00 to 17:30, last admission 16:30. Verify at the gate, and note that individual halls close to visitors without warning for conservation or filming.
stops.accessibility: The courtyard is level granite paving, but the throne hall is reached by two flights of wide stone steps. There is no ramp to the hall platform; the hall interior can be seen from the courtyard in front of the lower tier.
stops.insiderTip: Walk the length of the courtyard and read the stones in the front row rather than photographing the throne first. The markers spell out the entire Joseon bureaucracy; it is the clearest surviving diagram of how a Confucian state was actually arranged.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the courtyard by the west side and follow the signs downhill for about 250 metres, past Sajeongjeon and Sujeongjeon. The long wooden pavilion standing on an island in a rectangular pond, reached by three stone bridges, is Gyeonghoeru — our next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Gyeonghoeru Pavilion
stops.narration:
After the throne hall's granite formality, here is where the dynasty enjoyed itself. Gyeonghoeru, the name meaning something like the Pavilion of Joyful Meetings, is a two-storey timber hall on an artificial island in a large rectangular pond, reached over three stone bridges. The first version was finished in 1412; the one you see was rebuilt in 1867 with the rest of the palace. It is a National Treasure.

This was the court's banquet hall. Kings held feasts here for high officials and, more importantly, foreign envoys, which made it diplomacy in timber: the message to a visiting Chinese or Japanese mission was not just that Korea was wealthy but that it was cultured. The lower level is open on all sides, held up by 48 stone pillars; the upper floor has 35 rooms, and the king sat on the highest of its three levels. The proportions are loaded with numbers the court cared about: the twelve months, the eight trigrams of the I Ching, the twenty-four solar terms.

The twentieth century got its hands on it too: under colonial rule the Japanese authorities used the pavilion for their own banquets, including one for Ito Hirobumi, Japan's first resident-general in Korea, and at the 1915 industrial exhibition, the same event for which much of the palace was demolished, the pond was surrounded by shops and food stalls. The wall that once enclosed the pond was torn down and only put back between 2004 and 2005. The interior is normally closed, and special upstairs tours run only in certain seasons, never in midwinter, so plan on admiring it from the pond edge. In snow it is the best photograph in the palace.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Covered by the palace admission ticket, ₩3,000 for adults with the reductions and free days listed at the gate. Seeing the pavilion from the pond edge is included; the seasonal interior tours are free but require advance booking and are not offered in winter.
stops.openingHours: Viewable during palace hours, daily except Tuesdays, roughly 09:00 to 17:30 in November to January with last admission at 16:30. Interior tours run only in announced seasons — verify at the gate or on the palace website, and do not count on one in December or January.
stops.accessibility: The pond perimeter is level paving and fully step-free, and there are benches facing the pavilion. The bridges onto the island and the upper floor of the pavilion are stepped and not part of the normal visitor route.
stops.insiderTip: Come to the south-west corner of the pond, not the front. The pavilion sits at an angle to the light there, so the roof and the reflection line up and the 48 pillars all show at once — and if it has snowed, the island reads as a white silhouette.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk back east past the throne hall and follow the signs north across the palace, about 550 metres, to the tall building with the pagoda-shaped tower on its roofline standing at the top of the grounds. That is the National Folk Museum of Korea — our next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Frank Schulenburg, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: National Folk Museum of Korea
stops.narration:
This is where the walk stops being about kings. The National Folk Museum of Korea sits at the top of the palace grounds, its rooflines borrowed from temples around the country, and it collects the ordinary culture of ordinary Koreans: the farming calendar, the household, the rituals of a family from cradle to grave. Admission is free. Its own history is a colonial document: its predecessor, the Chosen Folk Art Museum, was founded in 1924, during Japanese rule, and the current institution traces to a national ethnology museum established by order of the US military government in November 1945 and opened in April 1946, in a building put up for the Japanese colonial administration. It moved onto these grounds in 1975 and into the present building in 1993.

Go in for the Confucian family, because it explains more about daily life in Korea than any palace room. Three permanent galleries: Koreans today, the year's seasonal customs, and life rituals. The Confucian inheritance shows up in the ancestor rites, jesa, offerings of food, wine and bows to your dead forebears on the anniversaries of their deaths and at the lunar new year and harvest festivals, which families still perform. It shows in the ceremonies marking a child's first birthday, a marriage and a sixtieth birthday, and in household shrines and the door and kitchen spirits, a folk layer older than both Confucianism and Buddhism.

Korea's religious landscape is not a set of exclusive boxes: one family may run ancestral rites, visit a Buddhist temple for the lantern festival and consult a shaman, or musok. In winter, November to February, the museum closes at 17:00 with last admission at 16:00, and it shuts on 1 January and the lunar new year and harvest holidays; individual galleries rotate out for maintenance. Then leave by the east gate onto Samcheong-ro.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free admission, but the museum stands inside the palace grounds, so you still need the ₩3,000 palace ticket to reach it. Verify at the gate; the free status and the palace fee are decided separately and can change.
stops.openingHours: Typically 09:00 to 18:00 from March to October and 09:00 to 17:00 from November to February, with last admission an hour before closing. Closed 1 January, the lunar new year and harvest holidays, and individual galleries close periodically for maintenance. Verify before you go.
stops.accessibility: Good. Lifts, accessible toilets and step-free routes link the permanent galleries, and the surrounding grounds are paved. The outdoor exhibition area is sometimes restricted on weekends and holidays.
stops.insiderTip: Skip the displays of aristocratic costume and spend your time in the gallery on seasonal customs. The farming calendar, the food preservation and the rites of the year explain why Korean daily life is still organised around the lunar calendar, long after the country industrialised.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the museum and exit the palace by the east gate onto Samcheong-ro, the street running along the palace wall. Turn left and walk south-east along it for about 800 metres, past the stone wall and the low galleries, and you are in Samcheong-dong — our next stop. It is a straight street walk with limited crossings, so give it ten minutes.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Nagyman, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Samcheong-dong
stops.narration:
The name Samcheong-dong means, roughly, the village of three pure things, and there are two stories about which three. One is that the mountains, the water and the people here were all clean. The other points to an old hall called Samcheongjeon, where three tablets stood: Taecheong, Sangcheong and Okcheong, names drawn from Taoism's Three Pure Ones. Both are given by Koreans, and neither is disproved.

What is certain is the recent history. Samcheong-dong is a hillside strip of small buildings and hanok, traditional Korean houses, timber-framed with tiled roofs, running along the palace's east side. From the 1970s and 1980s, artists and then galleries moved in, because the rents were low and the buildings small. Galleries pulled in cafes, cafes pulled in visitors, visitors pulled in higher rents. The reason it stayed low-rise is not taste: for decades the whole district was under height and development restrictions tied to the protected zone around the palace and, further north, the presidential compound of Cheong Wa Dae, the Blue House. That meant no towers. When Cheong Wa Dae opened to the public in 2022, after the president's office moved across town, it removed the most famous piece of restricted ground here, and the area is still adjusting.

Walk the street as a live argument. Look at what each hanok is being used for: gallery, cafe, dentist, tearoom, private house with a car parked in the courtyard. Sometimes the old building is genuinely the working space; sometimes it is a facade wrapped around a new interior. The National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art is a few minutes back toward the palace, and its permanent collections are free or nearly so. At the far end, a narrow alley turns off to your right between two walls: Bukchon-ro 11-gil, our next stop, restricted to visitors between 10:00 and 17:00 only.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk. Galleries, museums and cafes here set their own prices and hours, and many small galleries close one weekday — verify at each door.
stops.openingHours: The street is open at all times. Shops, galleries and cafes generally run mid-morning to early evening and several close on a weekday, so check individual doors. The adjacent Bukchon alley is restricted to visitors from 10:00 to 17:00.
stops.accessibility: The main street has a pavement but the slope is real, and side lanes are stepped and narrow. The street itself is manageable in a wheelchair with effort; most hanok interiors and galleries are entered over a step or a raised threshold.
stops.insiderTip: Look past the shopfronts at the rooflines. A genuine old hanok has a heavy curved tiled roof with visible wooden rafters underneath; a new building imitating one usually has a lighter, cleaner roof and a thicker, flatter wall. Once you can see the difference you will spot it all the way down to Insadong.
stops.nextStopDirections: Follow Samcheong-ro south-east to the end of the gallery strip and turn right into Bukchon-ro 11-gil, the narrow alley running between the hanok walls. Walk about 400 metres down the lane, past the gateways and the tea rooms, and you are in Bukchon Hanok Village — our next stop. It is a residential lane: keep your voice down, and stay out of it before 10:00 or after 17:00.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: travel oriented, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Bukchon Hanok Village
stops.narration:
You are standing in a neighbourhood, not a museum. Bukchon means "north village," the quarter north of the stream, between Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung palaces, and from the Joseon period it was where senior officials and the nobility kept houses. About 6,000 people live here; a recent year brought around six million visitors.

First, the building. A hanok is a single-storey Korean house on a timber frame, with paper-covered lattice doors and windows that soften the light, and, the part visitors always underestimate, ondol, underfloor heating: hot air from a kitchen fire channelled through stone flues under the floor, so the floor itself is the heater you sleep, sit and eat on. Add a heavy tiled roof. Most hanok were small; the grand courtyard houses on this lane are the exception. Second, the argument. In the 1960s through the 1980s, hanok were seen as obsolete and whole neighbourhoods were demolished; preservation policies followed, including measures from 2000 that subsidised repairs and restricted demolition. Critics, residents among them, say the rules froze people's property, made houses expensive to maintain and impossible to sell, and that a family died in 1990 when a hanok roof collapsed in heavy rain. Tourism then made the same houses valuable as guesthouses and photo studios.

Third, the rules. After a trial in November 2024 and enforcement from March 2025, the alleys around Bukchon-ro 11-gil, about 34,000 square metres designated a "red zone," may be visited only between 10:00 and 17:00. Outside those hours, tourism here can attract a ₩100,000 fine, rising for repeat offences, applied to foreign visitors exactly as to Koreans. Do not photograph through gateways into courtyards, or people as curiosities. The famous view down this lane, tiled roofs against Namsan, is one of eight the district lists as "Bukchon's eight views." Then head downhill toward Anguk, about 1.3 kilometres.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free, but it is a residential neighbourhood and no longer an unrestricted one. Visitor access in the red zone is limited to 10:00 to 17:00, and after-hours tourism can attract a ₩100,000 fine. Verify the current boundaries and hours before you come; rules were tightened in 2025 and 2026.
stops.openingHours: The red zone around Bukchon-ro 11-gil is open to visitors 10:00 to 17:00 only, with penalties outside those hours; Sundays are discouraged as a rest day for the alleys. Individual guesthouses, cafes and workshops keep their own hours.
stops.accessibility: Difficult, honestly. The lanes are steep, narrow, cobbled or stepped, and snow and ice make them genuinely dangerous — this is the hardest ground on the walk. There is no step-free route through the village; a walker with mobility needs should view it from Samcheong-ro or Bukchon-ro and skip the alley itself.
stops.insiderTip: Work out which way the light runs before you climb: the classic view down Bukchon-ro 11-gil faces south, so in winter the low sun rakes across the rooftops by early afternoon and the lane is in deep shadow after about 15:00. Come before then, and mind the residents' gates.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk south down the lane as Bukchon-ro 11-gil becomes Bukchon-ro, then follow the signs for Anguk Station downhill for about 1.3 kilometres — twenty minutes or so, past Gahoe-dong and the Bukchon culture centre. At the bottom, cross the main road at Anguk and walk into Insadong-gil. Our final stop is the old art street and the craft courtyard called Ssamzigil.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Insadong and Ssamzigil
stops.narration:
Insadong is the most instructive stop on this walk. It began about five hundred years ago as housing for government officials, close enough to the palaces and bureaucracies to walk to work, and it held Dohwaseo, the royal painting bureau that produced portraits of kings and painted the state's ceremonies. Its name was assembled in 1914 by the colonial administration, which merged two older districts, Gwanin-bang and Daesa-dong, and took a syllable from each.

That bureaucratic origin explains the odd shape of the street: Insadong-gil is one spine with a lattice of small alleys, because it grew as a residential quarter, not a shopping street. In the twentieth century the alleys filled with antique dealers and painters, and since the 1980s the state has curated the result. The city designated it a traditional culture street in 1988, the year Seoul hosted the Olympics, and in 2002 it became Korea's first designated cultural district. The country that bulldozed most of its traditional housing later legislated this street into a showcase of traditional culture.

Walk it as a series of small trades: brushes, ink, handmade paper, ceramics, wooden furniture, framed calligraphy, and in the alleys, tea. Korean tea culture, darye, the etiquette and ceremony of serving tea, was nursed in Goryeo court ritual and then in Buddhist monasteries, and what you can order here descends from it: omija, the five-flavour berry; daechu, jujube; ssanghwa, a bitter herbal brew. Then go to Ssamzigil, the craft complex on this street: it opened in 2004 as a single spiralling walkway climbing four floors around an open courtyard, no staircase, just a ramp of roughly seventy shops selling work by Korean makers. Look south toward Jogyesa, the head temple of the Jogye Order, Korea's main Buddhist school, whose lanterns fill the street at the Buddha's birthday.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk. Tea houses, galleries and Ssamzigil's shops are at their own menu and retail prices — a pot of traditional tea for one typically runs in the low tens of thousands of won, so check the menu before you sit down.
stops.openingHours: The street is open at all times; most shops and galleries run roughly 10:00 to 20:00 or later and many close one day a week. Ssamzigil is typically open 10:30 to 20:30 daily, though individual shops set their own hours — verify before a late run.
stops.accessibility: The main street is level and paved with kerbs at the crossings, and Ssamzigil has a lift as well as its spiral ramp, so it is genuinely step-free. The side alleys are narrow, uneven and often stepped; traditional tea houses mostly require squatting or sitting on the floor.
stops.insiderTip: Skip the first two blocks of souvenir shops and go into the alleys — that is where the tea houses, the brush-makers and the working galleries actually are. Look for the small paper and ink shops: they are the descendants of the trade that was here before any of this was a tourist street.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Anguk station is a few minutes south-east and Jonggak and Jongno 3-ga stations are a short walk west along the main road, all served by subway. Tea houses, noodle restaurants and bookshops along Insadong-gil and its alleys stay open into the evening — this is a good place to sit down, warm up and let the day finish.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Epicgenius, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
